subject: accountancy
chapter_title: Use of Spreadsheet in Business Applications

concepts.title: Payroll Components: Earnings and Deductions
concepts.definition: A salary bill rests on earnings heads and deduction heads. Earnings: Basic Pay from the pay scale plus Grade Pay, Dearness Pay merged into basic pay, Dearness Allowance granted periodically as a percentage to offset price-rise erosion, House Rent Allowance for leased accommodation, Transport Allowance for commuting, and any other declared allowance. Deductions: Professional Tax under state law, Provident Fund as a statutory social-security percentage, Tax Deducted at Source as the monthly slice of yearly income tax, loan instalment recovery and other recoveries.
concepts.formula: payroll_heads = earnings_basic plus allowances plus deductions_statutory plus recovery
concepts.key_idea: Earnings stack from basic pay upward; statutory and loan deductions come out before the employee is paid.

concepts.title: Effective Days and Basic Pay Earned
concepts.definition: Pay is earned only for days actually worked. Effective days present equal the days in the month less leave without pay and unauthorised absence, and the basic pay earned is the month's basic pay scaled by the ratio of effective days to days in the month -- so unpaid absence shrinks every allowance that follows, since all of them feed off the earned figure.
concepts.key_idea: Scale the month's basic pay by effective days over calendar days; every later head keys off this earned amount.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, BPE and NOEDP formulas (approx lines 126-168)

solution_steps.explain: multiplying basic pay by the effective-day fraction earns pay only for days worked

concepts.title: Allowance Computation: DA and HRA as Percentages
concepts.definition: Percentage allowances apply to the earned basic pay: Dearness Allowance at the rate notified for the month, House Rent Allowance at a rate that depends on employee category -- the template uses 40 per cent of earned pay for supervisory staff and 30 per cent for non-supervisory staff, with nil for consultants. Transport allowance is either a fixed amount or a percentage. Once the applicable rate is picked, every allowance is that percentage of the earned figure.
concepts.key_idea: Pick the applicable percentage by category, then take that slice of the earned basic pay.

concepts.title: Gross Salary Assembly
concepts.definition: Total earnings, or gross salary, aggregate every earning head of the month: the basic pay earned plus dearness allowance, house rent allowance and transport allowance. The payroll template sums these columns for each employee, and the gross figure becomes the base from which deductions are subtracted.
concepts.key_idea: Gross salary is the sum of earned basic pay and every allowance of the month.

concepts.title: Deductions and Net Salary
concepts.definition: Deductions comprise the provident fund computed as a percentage of earned pay, tax deducted at source -- essentially the yearly income tax spread over twelve months -- and fixed loan instalment recoveries. Their sum is total deductions, and subtracting it from total earnings leaves the net salary, the amount actually paid into the employee's bank account through the bank advice.
concepts.key_idea: Take gross salary, strip the provident fund, tax and loan recoveries, and what remains is the take-home pay.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, TD and NS formulas (approx lines 141-180)

concepts.title: Nested IF for Employee-Type Rules
concepts.definition: The payroll template implements category rules with a nested IF: for house rent allowance, a supervisory employee takes 40 per cent of earned pay, a non-supervisory employee 30 per cent, and anything else nil; for transport allowance the same structure returns 1000 for supervisory, 500 for non-supervisory and zero otherwise. The rate cells carry absolute addresses so that copying the formula down the column never shifts the reference.
concepts.formula: type_rule = nested IF picks the rate or fixed amount by employee type
concepts.key_idea: An IF inside an IF routes each employee category to its own rate, else to zero.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, template columns I and J with nested IF (approx lines 221-232, 306-318)

solution_steps.explain: the outer IF tests supervisory, the inner IF tests non-supervisory, and the final else returns zero

concepts.title: Template Design: Direct Values versus Formulas
concepts.definition: Every spreadsheet application starts with a template: plan the column layout, decide for each column whether a value is typed directly or produced by a formula, and mark the cells holding formulas. The payroll sheet, for instance, takes employee number, name, type, deduction days and basic pay as direct entries, while effective days, earned pay, allowances, deductions and net salary are computed. Once laid out, entering values makes results appear immediately.
concepts.key_idea: Decide column by column what is typed and what is computed -- the template then calculates itself.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, template design and Figure 3.1 (approx lines 181-269)

solution_steps.explain: identity, attendance and basic pay are typed; effective days onward are computed by formula

concepts.title: Acquisition Cost: Cost to Use an Asset
concepts.definition: An asset enters the books at its acquisition cost, not merely its invoice price: purchase value plus transportation, installation and pre-operating expenses together form the cost to use. Depreciable allocations build on this total, alongside the salvage value -- the amount realisable at the end of the asset's useful life -- while free-hold land usually carries no depreciation at all.
concepts.key_idea: Capitalise the purchase with transport, installation and pre-operating spending to get the cost that depreciates.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, acquisition cost formula and cost-to-use column (approx lines 463-477, 569-572)
question_patterns: a machine costs Rs 100000 with installation of Rs 8000 and pre-operating expenses of Rs 2000; find the cost to use

solution_steps.explain: purchase cost plus installation and pre-operating expenses forms the total cost put to use

concepts.title: Straight Line Method of Depreciation
concepts.definition: Under the Straight Line Method the asset loses an equal slice of value every year: the total depreciable amount -- acquisition cost minus salvage value -- divides evenly over the expected useful life. The depreciation rate expresses the annual charge as a percentage of the depreciable amount. Excel computes it with the SLN function, and the total depreciation over the asset's life equals acquisition cost less salvage value.
concepts.key_idea: Split cost-minus-salvage evenly across the useful life; every year carries the same charge.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, SLM formulas and SLN usage (approx lines 462-505)

solution_steps.explain: acquisition cost less salvage value is the amount the asset must lose over its life
dividing the depreciable amount by the years of useful life gives the equal annual depreciation

concepts.title: Written Down Value Method of Depreciation
concepts.definition: The Written Down Value or Declining Balance method charges each year's depreciation on the current book value, so the charge shrinks as the asset ages. Excel's DB function takes cost, salvage, life, the period concerned and the months in the first year. For a constant rate, the book value after some years is the cost multiplied by the surviving fraction -- one minus the rate -- raised to those years.
concepts.key_idea: Each year the rate bites the shrinking book value, so value after n years is cost times the surviving fraction to the nth power.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, WDV method and DB function (approx lines 597-643, 796-802)

solution_steps.action: apply the declining rate over the years
solution_steps.explain: multiplying cost by the surviving fraction raised to the years in use leaves the written down value

concepts.title: Fixed Asset Schedule: Gross Block, Depreciation and Net Block
concepts.section: 3.2.2.3 Schedule Forming Part of the Balance Sheet
concepts.definition: The fixed asset schedule reported with the balance sheet carries three blocks per asset class. Gross block rolls forward from the April 1 opening by adding additions and subtracting deductions to reach the March 31 closing. Depreciation rolls forward the same way, its additions transferred from the depreciation computation sheet. Net block is gross block minus depreciation, on both dates, and the whole schedule can be laid out as spreadsheet columns with rolling formulas.
concepts.key_idea: Roll each block forward with additions and deductions, then gross block minus depreciation leaves the net block.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, schedule columns E, I, J, K (approx lines 819-912)
question_patterns: opening gross block is Rs 500000 with additions Rs 50000 and no deductions; depreciation stands at Rs 245000; find the net block

solution_steps.explain: opening gross plus additions less deductions gives the closing gross block
opening depreciation plus the year's charge less deductions gives the closing depreciation
closing gross block less closing depreciation is the net block reported in the balance sheet

concepts.title: Loan Repayment Schedule with PMT
concepts.definition: A loan of principal borrowed at a stated rate for a stated period repays through periodic instalments, computed with Excel's PMT function: rate is the interest per period, nper the total payments whose unit must match the rate, pv the loan amount, and fv the end balance -- taken as zero, because with regular repayments nothing remains payable at the end. Type 1 pays at the period's beginning and 0 at its end; a yearly instalment divides by twelve for monthly payment.
concepts.formula: loan_terms = principal plus rate per period plus nper payments plus fv of zero
concepts.key_idea: PMT spreads principal and interest into equal payments, with future value zero once the loan is fully repaid.
concepts.textbook_ref: leca103.txt, section 3.3 and PMT parameters (approx lines 923-1039)
question_patterns: why is the future value taken as zero in loan repayment calculations

solution_steps.explain: rate per period, matching payment count, loan amount as present value, zero future value, and the payment-timing type
regular instalments extinguish the debt by the end of the term, so the balance due, and hence fv, is zero
